title: Bottles and Breastfeeding Equipment Screening Enhancement Act
official_title: An Act to amend the Bottles and Breastfeeding Equipment Screening Act to require hygienic handling of breast milk and baby formula by security screening personnel of the Transportation Security Administration and personnel of private security companies providing security screening, and for other purposes.
likelihoodReason: Became Public Law 119-41 on November 25, 2025. Passed the Senate on May 14, 2025 and the House on November 17, 2025.
summary: Requires the TSA to issue guidance for the hygienic handling of breast milk, baby formula, and related items during airport security re-screening, and orders an audit of how well it is followed.
brief: Requires TSA guidance on hygienic handling of breast milk and baby formula during airport screening, plus an Inspector General audit.

top_lines.headline: Hygienic Screening of Infant Items
subs: TSA must issue hygienic-handling guidance within 90 days
Covers breast milk, baby formula, infant water, and juice
Applies to TSA and private screening personnel

top_lines.headline: Compliance Audit
subs: DHS Inspector General audit of compliance within 1 year

items.main: Names the Act the “Bottles and Breastfeeding Equipment Screening Enhancement Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect (49 U.S.C. 40101 note).

sections.label: Section 2 — Hygienic Handling of Breast Milk and Baby Formula During Aviation Security Screening

items.main: Amends the Bottles and Breastfeeding Equipment Screening Act (Public Law 114-293) to add two new sections requiring hygienic handling of infant items during TSA screening and an Inspector General audit.
items.detail: Adds new SEC. 3 and SEC. 4 to the Act (49 U.S.C. 44901 note). New SEC. 3: within 90 days of enactment, and every five years thereafter if appropriate, the TSA Administrator must issue or update guidance — developed with nationally recognized maternal health organizations — to minimize contamination risk for breast milk, baby formula, purified deionized water for infants, and juice (plus the ice packs, freezer packs, and gel packs used to cool them) subject to re-screening or additional screening; the guidance applies to TSA screeners and private screening company personnel under section 44920 of title 49. New SEC. 4: within one year of enactment, the DHS Inspector General must report to the House Homeland Security Committee and the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee an audit of compliance with sections 2 and 3, including the effect of screening technologies such as bottled liquid scanners and the rate at which such items are denied entry into the sterile area.

gaps: The bill requires hygienic-handling guidance but leaves the specific contamination standards to the TSA rather than setting them in law.
It mandates an audit of compliance but specifies no consequence if screeners fail to follow the guidance.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Swalwell
featured_quotes.text: Air travel with children is a nightmare, and I am just talking for the nonparents who have to deal with them at an airport. For parents, it is hell. It is like an Olympic sport. It is like going through a gauntlet dragging little kids who just want to be attached to tablets or anything but the directions that you are giving to them to hopefully get them from the entrance of the airport to the plane. Oftentimes with little kids, you have, in transit with them, a mother who is breastfeeding.

added: TSA hygienic-handling guidance for breast milk, baby formula, infant water, and juice during screening (new Section 3 of Public Law 114-293)
DHS Inspector General audit of compliance within one year (new Section 4)
